# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review of the Halden reduced-hours working paper

**Bottom line:** I checked every number and they are internally consistent. The table sums, weighted means and percentage changes all reproduce. The problem is that the headline conclusions go well beyond what the design and numbers support. In places the paper's own data point the other way, especially on "sector-general."

## 1. The output-per-hour gain is built into the arithmetic

Output per scheduled hour is defined as the output index divided by 0.8. Any index above 80 therefore shows a per-hour "gain."
- An organisation whose output fell 15% would still report +6% per hour.
- So "gains in output per hour in every sector" is not an independent finding. It only says every sector's index stayed above 80.
- The Limitations section leans on the result's "size and consistency across sectors." That consistency is guaranteed by the calculation, so it can't offset the limitations.

The quantity that actually varies is the **output index itself**. It fell in five of six sectors.

## 2. The retail and hospitality data contradict "sector-general"

- **Output fell.** Retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%. With pay unchanged, unit labour cost rose about 7.4%. In a thin-margin sector that is a material cost, not "close to baseline."
- **Half the retail organisations quit.** Three of the six reverted to the old schedule, as did 2 of 5 healthcare-administration organisations. All five reversions came from the two weakest sectors. Every knowledge-work organisation continued.
- **Small sample, no uncertainty.** The sector has 6 organisations and 300 staff. The paper reports no confidence intervals or spread across organisations.
- **Coverage costs are unreported.** Seventeen organisations used staggered days off "to maintain coverage." The paper doesn't say whether headcount, overtime or agency staff changed. If coverage was bought with extra staff, output per hour of the original staff overstates the efficiency gain.
- **Narrow sector range.** The six sectors are mostly office and knowledge work. There is no manufacturing, logistics, construction or frontline care.

The Discussion says "even there output per hour rose by 16.4%." That reads a sector where output fell and half the organisations reverted as confirmation. A defensible conclusion would be something like: *the model held up in knowledge-work sectors and was considerably harder in customer-facing ones.*

## 3. Outcome measurement

**The output index is subjective and has an obvious anchor.**
- It was filled in by managers who ran the pilot, in organisations that volunteered because they expected success.
- It was scored against an anchor of 100 = "unchanged," using whatever records each organisation happened to keep.
- Every sector lands between 93 and 101. That is consistent with real stability, but also with anchoring on 100.
- The paper should report what records were used, any objective sub-measures, and the distribution across organisations.

**Seasonality is handled inconsistently.**
- Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year "to remove seasonality."
- Output, sick days and resignations are compared with the *preceding* six months, so they are not.
- If the pilot ran roughly spring to autumn 2023, the baseline covered winter. That affects sick days (flu season) and retail and hospitality output.

**Part of the sick-day drop is mechanical.**
- A four-day schedule has 20% fewer working days on which anyone can be absent.
- If absence is counted in days, about 4.4 → 3.5 is expected with no change in health.
- The genuine reduction is therefore closer to 20% than 36%, unless absence is measured per scheduled day.

**Actual hours.** The paper says actual hours were not collected "from all organisations." So some data exist and should be reported. Any gap between scheduled and actual hours inflates the per-hour figure directly.

## 4. Revenue

- **Nominal, not real.** +1.4% is nominal. Depending on the countries involved, 2023 inflation was roughly 4–7% in most advanced economies. That makes +1.4% a **real decline**, which is the opposite of "no sign that output was sacrificed."
- **Missing reporters.** Nine organisations did not report revenue. The paper should say which sectors they were in and whether any of them reverted.

## 5. Wellbeing results

- **Energy faded by half.** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three and only 0.29 SD by month six. That pattern fits a novelty effect. The Discussion reports "more energy" without noting the fade, which also bears on Limitation 5 (duration).
- **The productivity self-rating is weak.** "Rating own productivity 'higher than before'" has no baseline, and the question is leading. Workers who personally benefit also have an obvious incentive to answer favourably.
- **The resignation drop has other explanations.** It could partly reflect a cooling 2023 labour market. Staff may also have delayed leaving to keep a favourable arrangement. The six months of resignations were annualised, which makes this figure particularly noisy.

## 6. Denominators and selection

- **Continuation rate.** The 92% figure excludes the 9 organisations that withdrew before starting, "chiefly for scheduling reasons," which is exactly the kind of organisation for which the model may not work. Against the 70 that enrolled, continuation is 80%.
- **Interview attrition.** 58 of 61 managers were interviewed. Were the three missing among the reverters?
- **What "continue" means.** Only 18 organisations made the change permanent. The other 38 "continued," which could mean an extended trial.

## 7. Causal claims

- **Fatigue versus process changes.** The Discussion calls reduced fatigue "the most plausible single explanation." The paper's only evidence on mechanism, the manager interviews, points instead to process changes: fewer meetings, focus blocks, simpler approvals. These were described as changes managers "had wanted to make for years." This matters for policy, because those changes are available without cutting hours.
- **Continuation doesn't show productivity.** The claim that "the high continuation rate is itself evidence" is weak on productivity specifically. Reverting has real costs, such as morale and retention signals, and organisations self-selected for enthusiasm. Continuation shows the arrangement was popular and tolerable, not that output held.

## 8. The Limitations section undercuts itself

The listed limitations all bias in the **same favourable direction**: self-selection, manager-reported outcomes, scheduled rather than actual hours, and no control group. Biases that point the same way don't cancel, and consistency across sectors can't rule them out.

## What the data do support

- Mostly knowledge-work organisations that volunteered and prepared for two months kept manager-reported output within a few percent of baseline on a 20% cut in scheduled hours.
- Employees reported large wellbeing gains, though these partly faded.
- Most organisations chose to keep the arrangement.

That is a worthwhile result. It does not show that the model is "sector-general" or that productivity rose 23%.

## Suggested changes

- **Lead with the output index, not output per hour.** Report the distribution across organisations with uncertainty.
- **Revise the conclusions.** Drop "sector-general," report retail and hospitality as a difficult case, and present revenue in real terms.
- **Fix the comparisons.** Adjust sick days per scheduled day, and give seasonal comparisons for output and absence.
- **Report what exists.** Include the partial actual-hours data and coverage and headcount changes.
- **Rebalance the explanation.** Treat process change and fatigue as competing explanations, not a primary one plus a contributor.
